subtopics.title: Studying genre across texts

outcomes.text: Study one chosen genre option, tragedy or comedy, through four texts: a Shakespeare play, a further drama text, a poetry text and a prose text.
Read texts in their genre by connecting them to other texts, contexts of writing and reception, and modern readers' interpretations.
Weigh the significance of a text by combining its construction, relevant contexts, links to other texts and possible interpretations.

subtopics.title: Aspects of tragedy: the hero and the world

outcomes.text: Tell classical tragedy about public figures from domestic tragedy about ordinary people.
Explore the places and times in which a tragedy is set.
Follow the protagonist's journey toward death: flaws, pride, folly, blindness and insight, learning, mixed good and evil.
Explore the tragic villain or opponent who shapes the hero's fortune and shares blame for the downfall.
Explore the presence of fate and the sense that the hero's end is inevitable.

subtopics.title: Aspects of tragedy: structure and effect

outcomes.text: Explain how the hero's behaviour creates chaos and affects the lives of others.
Weigh the significance of violence, revenge, humour and moments of happiness.
Trace structure from complication to catastrophe, order to disorder, climax to resolution, with plots and sub-plots.
Analyse how language heightens the tragedy.
Explain how tragedy affects the audience through pity and fear and comments on the real world and the human condition.

subtopics.title: Set texts for tragedy

outcomes.text: Study one Shakespeare tragedy from Othello or King Lear.
Study one further drama from Death of a Salesman, Richard II or A Streetcar Named Desire.
Study one prose text from The Great Gatsby, Tess of the D'Urbervilles or The Remains of the Day, and one poetry text from Hardy, Keats or the AQA tragedy anthology.

subtopics.title: Aspects of comedy: the characters and the world

outcomes.text: Tell types of comedy apart: romantic drama, satire and comedy of manners.
Explore the places and times in which a comedy is set.
Follow the protagonists' journey to knowledge and happiness, through mistakes and misunderstandings to joy.
Explore the comic villain or rival whose disruption is finally curtailed, and the sense that all will end well.
Explain how the hero's behaviour affects mainly themselves and a few others, unlike tragedy.

subtopics.title: Aspects of comedy: structure and effect

outcomes.text: Explore human folly, trickery and gullibility, and clowns, exaggeration, stereotypes and pomposity.
Explore disguise, escape, discovery and elements of the supernatural.
Trace structure from disorder to order, rule and misrule, competition and reconciled opposites, with complex plots and sub-plots.
Analyse how language heightens comedy through wit and wordplay, and how comedy draws attention to itself.
Explain how comedy invites laughter at human absurdity and a joyful sense that good resolutions are possible.

subtopics.title: Set texts for comedy

outcomes.text: Study one Shakespeare comedy from The Taming of the Shrew or Twelfth Night.
Study one further drama from She Stoops to Conquer, Educating Rita or The Importance of Being Earnest.
Study one prose text from Emma, Wise Children or Small Island, and one poetry text from Betjeman, Chaucer or the AQA comedy anthology.

subtopics.title: Literary genres component

outcomes.text: Study one genre option, tragedy or comedy, through three texts: a Shakespeare play, a second drama text and one further text, with one non-Shakespeare text written before 1900.
Meet the closed-book exam where set texts cannot be taken in.

subtopics.title: Texts and genres component

outcomes.text: Study one option, crime writing or political and social protest writing, through three texts: a post-2000 prose text, a poetry text and one further text, with one pre-1900.
Respond to an unseen passage from poetry, prose, drama or literary non-fiction.
Meet the open-book exam, taking unannotated copies of set texts.

subtopics.title: Elements of crime writing: crime, criminal and detection

outcomes.text: Tell types of crime text apart: detective fiction, post-modern novel, revenge tragedy, account of a life lost to crime.
Explore the settings of criminal action and its pursuit, in place and time.
Explore the nature of crimes and criminals, their motives and actions, including violence, murder, theft and betrayal.
Follow the detection and investigation that lead to capture or punishment, and the creation of the criminal and the detective hero.
Judge how far a text has moral purpose and restores order, and the expectation that the criminal is punished.

subtopics.title: Elements of crime writing: justice, structure and effect

outcomes.text: Explore guilt, remorse, confession and the desire for forgiveness, and the victims and their suffering.
Explore motifs of love, money, danger and death, and punishment, justice, retribution, injustice and the legal system.
Trace structure through crises to order, with focus on plotting.
Analyse crime registers: criminal, legal and police language.
Explain how crime writing comments on society in a historical period and affects readers through suspense, repugnance, excitement and relief.

subtopics.title: Set texts for crime writing

outcomes.text: Study three texts: a post-2000 prose text, a pre-1900 poetry text and one further text, from the crime list including Atkinson, Christie, Coleridge, Dickens, Greene, McEwan, Shakespeare's Hamlet and Walsh.

topics.title: 4.2.2 Elements of political and social protest writing

subtopics.title: Elements of protest writing: power and politics

outcomes.text: Tell types of protest text apart: post-modern novel, science fiction, satirical poetry, historical and political drama.
Explore the settings, real or imagined, where power struggles play out, in place and time.
Explore the nature of the power struggle: behaviour of those with and without power.
Explore the pursuit of power, rebellion, warfare and the workings of ruling political classes.
Explore corruption, conspiracy and control.

subtopics.title: Elements of protest writing: society, structure and effect

outcomes.text: Connect the smaller world to the larger world and focus on human organisation at home, work and in government.
Explore gender politics and social class.
Trace how political tensions are heightened and perhaps resolved in a text's structure.
Analyse how language is used in the worlds created.
Explain how protest writing comments on society in a historical period and invites reflection on our own world.

subtopics.title: Set texts for protest writing

outcomes.text: Study three texts: a post-2000 prose text, a poetry text and one further text, one pre-1900, from the list including Atwood, Blake, Crace, Dickens, Ganeshananthan, Harrison, Hosseini, Ibsen and Shakespeare's Henry IV Part I.

subtopics.title: Critical theory and independent reading

outcomes.text: Read widely and independently, applying different critical methods to literary texts.
Use the AQA Critical anthology on narrative, feminist, Marxist, eco-critical and post-colonial theory, and literary value and the canon.
Write about two texts, one poetry and one prose, each linked to a different anthology section.
Write two essays of 1250-1500 words, one conventional and one possibly re-creative with a commentary linking it to the base text and anthology.
Write a conventional essay that debates potential meanings using critical ideas.
Write a re-creative piece that fills narrative gaps or uses a new voice, with a commentary on choices that led to a critical reading.

subtopics.title: Choosing texts for independent study

outcomes.text: Choose one prose and one poetry text that allow access to a range of critical views, none from the exam set text lists.
Choose a poetry text that is a long narrative poem or single-author collection, studying it whole and writing on at least two poems in a conventional essay.
Choose single-author short story collections, or one influential text in translation, treated as the writer's own words.
